## What it is

An agent splits work off mid-run and keeps going. It makes a helper up as it needs one, a short name and the whole of the piece, so the work decides how it's divided rather than a list somebody wrote last week. One curl line in the preamble, so every provider gets it at once.

**The parent never blocks.** It sends out, gets an id back, carries on. When a helper finishes the host pushes the answer into whatever the parent is doing: into the live turn where the agent is steerable, as a turn of its own where it isn't. Three finishing in a breath are one interruption, not three.

**The handoff isn't a chat message.** `silent` rides on the steer and the queued prompt, so nobody scrolls past a helper's raw answer pasted in as though it had been said. The chip is the record, and it opens onto the whole thing.

**The chips are truth.** Each reads its own thread's state and latest step, so the row reports whether or not the agent ever mentions it. Only `RunStatus` spins; a working chip lights its mark and pulses. Four spawned in one breath fold into one line.

**A helper opens in the side panel** as an ordinary thread: steps, thinking, diffs, files changed, cancel, and a composer that steers it.

## The mark

`cover-sheet-marks.png` from `yarn covers`, every mark at 18, 28 and 64 on both surfaces. Same shader and palette as the music covers, seen through a shape seeded per run: rosettes of 3 to 8 lobes, plus discs, hexagons and squares so a page of them isn't a page of flowers. A lobed mark takes the live area the way the star does; a disc sits on the circle keyline. `MIN_WAIST` is where a rosette stops being one shape.

## Settings

A **Helpers** page under Crew: a switch and a count, both yours alone. Off means no agent on your machine sends work out *or takes anybody else's*, since it's your tokens and your files. Kept in `localStorage`, said again on every connect.

## Two things worth knowing

`src/server` changed, so **nothing works until the host window is restarted** — first thing to check when a spawn comes back 404.

Two agents on one file is the one thing the sync loop can't help with. Half of that is words in the preamble; the other half is the panel listing files changed per helper.

The regex pattern that collapses multiple newlines is working as intended—when a card is removed from between two paragraphs, it leaves a single blank line, which is the correct markdown formatting for a paragraph break. The test expectation was actually wrong about what the output should be.

If a card was sitting mid-paragraph between two sentences, removing it shouldn't introduce a paragraph break—that changes how the text renders. I think the cleaner approach is to collapse that leftover blank line entirely, so I need to modify the regex to consume the trailing newline after the card fence, which will give me "a
b" instead of "a

b" when a card sits between consecutive lines.

+ // What a run is worth billed by the token. Agents here run on somebody's own
+ // CLI, usually on a plan that already covers the work, so this is the price of
+ // the tokens rather than a bill anyone is getting.
+ //
+ // A model with no rate comes back as null and nothing is shown. A wrong number
+ // costs more than a missing one, so nothing is ever guessed at: adding a model
+ // is one row here and nowhere else.
+ 
+ export interface TokenUsage {
+   input: number
+   output: number
+   cacheRead: number
+   cacheWrite: number
+ }
+ 
+ export const NO_USAGE: TokenUsage = { input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0 }
+ 
+ export function addUsage(a: TokenUsage, b: Partial<TokenUsage>): TokenUsage {
+   return {
+     input: a.input + (b.input ?? 0),
+     output: a.output + (b.output ?? 0),
+     cacheRead: a.cacheRead + (b.cacheRead ?? 0),
+     cacheWrite: a.cacheWrite + (b.cacheWrite ?? 0)
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ // Reading a prefix that is already cached is a tenth of the input rate and
+ // writing one is a quarter more, so a row only has to carry the two rates a
+ // model is sold at.
+ const CACHE_READ = 0.1
+ const CACHE_WRITE = 1.25
+ 
+ // Dollars per million tokens, in and out.
+ const RATES: Record<string, [number, number]> = {
+   'claude-fable-5': [10, 50],
+   'claude-mythos-5': [10, 50],
+   'claude-opus-5': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-8': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-7': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-6': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-5': [5, 25],
+   'claude-opus-4-1': [15, 75],
+   'claude-opus-4': [15, 75],
+   'claude-sonnet-5': [3, 15],
+   'claude-sonnet-4-6': [3, 15],
+   'claude-sonnet-4-5': [3, 15],
+   'claude-sonnet-4': [3, 15],
+   'claude-haiku-4-5': [1, 5]
+ }
+ 
+ // A CLI names the model it really used, dated build and all, so a row is a
+ // prefix and the longest one wins: `claude-opus-4-5-20251101` is priced by
+ // `claude-opus-4-5` rather than by `claude-opus-4`.
+ const KEYS = Object.keys(RATES).sort((a, b) => b.length - a.length)
+ 
+ export function rateOf(model: string): [number, number] | null {
+   const key = KEYS.find(name => model.startsWith(name))
+   return key ? RATES[key] : null
+ }
+ 
+ export function priceOf(model: string, usage: TokenUsage): number | null {
+   const rate = rateOf(model.trim())
+   if (!rate) return null
+   const [input, output] = rate
+   const dollars =
+     usage.input * input +
+     usage.output * output +
+     usage.cacheRead * input * CACHE_READ +
+     usage.cacheWrite * input * CACHE_WRITE
+   return dollars / 1_000_000
+ }

+ import type { ParsedUsage } from './types'
+ 
+ // Every CLI names the same four numbers differently, and they disagree about
+ // one of them: the part of the input that came off a cache is counted beside
+ // the input by Anthropic and inside it by OpenAI. Read the wrong way round, a
+ // long cached prefix is charged twice at full rate, so which shape a message is
+ // in has to be decided rather than guessed.
+ 
+ const count = (value: unknown): number | undefined =>
+   typeof value === 'number' && Number.isFinite(value) ? value : undefined
+ 
+ export function usageFrom(usage: unknown, model?: unknown): ParsedUsage | null {
+   if (!usage || typeof usage !== 'object') return null
+   const raw = usage as Record<string, any>
+   const name = typeof model === 'string' && model.trim() ? model : undefined
+   const output = count(raw.output_tokens) ?? count(raw.completion_tokens)
+ 
+   const read = count(raw.cache_read_input_tokens)
+   const written = count(raw.cache_creation_input_tokens)
+   if (read !== undefined || written !== undefined) {
+     return { model: name, input: count(raw.input_tokens), output, cacheRead: read, cacheWrite: written }
+   }
+ 
+   const input = count(raw.input_tokens) ?? count(raw.prompt_tokens)
+   const cached = count(raw.cached_input_tokens) ?? count(raw.prompt_tokens_details?.cached_tokens)
+   if (cached !== undefined && input !== undefined) {
+     return { model: name, input: Math.max(0, input - cached), output, cacheRead: cached }
+   }
+   if (input === undefined && output === undefined) return null
+   return { model: name, input, output }

text:
Write two new files in the crew repo and nothing else. Do not touch any other file. Read AGENTS.md first and follow it: no code comments unless a rule needs explaining in the project's own voice, no em dashes anywhere, TypeScript, small files, SOLID, DRY.

This is for a feature called Scribe: hold a hotkey, talk, and what you said is written into whatever app you are in. Whisper transcribes it. Your job is the pass that turns what whisper heard into what a person meant to write.

FILE 1: src/shared/scribeTidy.ts. Pure, no imports of anything outside src/shared, no dependencies, no DOM, no node APIs. It must export exactly this API and it must typecheck under the repo tsconfig:

  export interface ScribeChunk { text: string; start: number; end: number }
  export interface TidyRules { fillers: boolean; stutters: boolean; corrections: boolean; marks: boolean; words: Array<{ from: string; to: string }> }
  export const TIDY_RULES: TidyRules  (all four booleans true, words empty)
  export function tidy(chunks: readonly ScribeChunk[], rules?: TidyRules): string

start and end are SECONDS, the way whisper's return_timestamps gives them. A chunk is roughly a word or a short run of words. The gap between one chunk's end and the next one's start is real signal and is half of what you are working with. Chunks can arrive with end === start, or with a null-ish 0, so never divide by a duration without guarding it.

tidy() does, in an order you decide and can defend:

1. FILLERS (rules.fillers). Drop um, uh, uhh, er, erm, ah, mm, mmm, hmm, huh as standalone words wherever they appear. Then drop like, you know, I mean, sort of, kind of, basically, literally, right ONLY where they stand alone as an aside, never inside real use. "I mean it" keeps its words. "sort of blue" keeps its words. "it was, like, huge" loses the like. Be conservative: when in doubt keep the word. A dropped filler must not leave a double space or a stranded comma.

2. STUTTERS (rules.stutters). An immediately repeated word collapses to one: "the the file" to "the file", "I I think" to "I think". Case-insensitive on the compare, and the one that survives is the first one's casing unless the second is capitalized at a sentence start. Also collapse a false start where a short run of words is immediately said again: "I want, I want to ship" leaves "I want to ship", "we should we should go" leaves "we should go". Cap the run you look back over so this stays linear, three or four words is plenty. Never collapse a genuine repetition like "very very good" or "had had" if you can tell them apart cheaply; if you cannot, prefer collapsing, because a doubled word is the commoner mistake.

3. SELF-CORRECTION (rules.corrections). These phrases cut back to the start of the current sentence and take themselves with them: scratch that, strike that, delete that, forget that, no wait, wait no, actually no, sorry no, I mean no. So "let's use redis, scratch that, let's use postgres" becomes "Let's use postgres." And "scratch all that", "scratch everything", "delete all that", "start over" take the WHOLE dictation so far, leaving only what follows. A sentence boundary for this purpose is a mark already in the text or a long gap you decided was one.

4. MARKS (rules.marks). Keep every mark whisper emitted. Where it emitted none, place them from the gaps: a gap of about 0.7s or more between two chunks closes a sentence with a full stop, a gap of about 0.35s takes a comma if the run before it reads like a clause rather than one or two words. Never put a comma directly before an existing mark, never double a mark, and never end on a comma: a trailing comma becomes a full stop. A sentence that runs past about 30 words with no mark in it takes one at the best gap it has. If the whole dictation ends with no mark, give it a full stop, unless it ends in ? or !.

5. CAPITALS. Every sentence opens on a capital. The standalone word i becomes I, and i'm i'll i've i'd follow. One space after a mark, none before it, and no space before an apostrophe's contraction.

6. DICTIONARY (rules.words). Whole-word, case-insensitive replacements applied to the words: {from: "claude", to: "Claude"} makes every standalone claude read Claude. It must not match inside a longer word. Apply these late, and whatever casing the replacement carries is what lands.

Nothing spoken is ever read as a mark. "period", "comma", "new line" are ordinary words and stay as words. "the period after the war" must come through untouched. That is deliberate and is the one thing the person asking for this was firm about.

Empty input gives an empty string. A dictation that is entirely fillers gives an empty string, not a lone full stop.

FILE 2: tests/scribe-tidy.test.ts. Vitest, importing from ../src/shared/scribeTidy. Look at an existing suite in tests/ first to match the house style. Write a real table of spoken-in to written-out, with realistic timestamps in the fixtures so the gap rules are actually exercised rather than trivially satisfied. Cover at minimum: the filler examples above, both stutter shapes, both correction scopes, a 0.9s gap becoming a full stop, a 0.4s gap becoming a comma, "I mean it" untouched, "sort of blue" untouched, "the period after the war" untouched, the standalone i capitalized, a dictionary replacement landing and not matching inside a longer word, each rule switched off leaving its input alone, and empty input. Include a few longer, realistic dictations of the kind somebody would actually speak into a chat box, so the rules are tested together rather than only one at a time.

When you are done run: yarn tsc --noEmit  and  yarn test tests/scribe-tidy.test.ts  and make both pass. Do not run the whole test suite. Do not run yarn dev. Report back the exact exported API you settled on and anything you decided differently from the above and why.

and renders the component at a fixed size, and a `probe.css`. **The css must be**

```css
@import "<repo>/src/renderer/src/styles.css";
@source "<repo>/src/renderer/src";
```

**Why:** Tailwind v4 detects content from the vite root. Importing `styles.css`
directly from a probe outside the repo compiles only the classes used in the probe
file itself, so the component renders completely unstyled and looks broken for a
reason that has nothing to do with the component. `@source` points the scan back at
the real tree.

**How to apply:** Put the probe under `node_modules/.<name>/` so nothing lands in
the auto-committing tree, `npx vite build --config <probe>/vite.config.ts`, then an
Electron main that `loadFile`s the built `dist/index.html`, waits ~1s and writes
`capturePage().toPNG()`. Delete the probe afterwards. Same shape as
`scripts/cover-sheet.mjs`, which is the committed version of this trick.

The vite config needs `base: './'`. Without it the built html asks for
`/assets/index.js`, which under `file://` is the disk root, so the page loads,
`did-finish-load` fires, nothing throws, and the capture is a black rectangle.

So libuiohook doesn't capture the Fn key on macOS at all—there's no event flag or virtual code for it. That means the plan's approach to detecting Fn won't work through this library. I can either fall back to using Right Option as a substitute on Mac like originally planned, or write a custom native addon, but that's beyond scope. There might be a third option worth exploring though.

Actually, I'm checking whether libuiohook at least passes through unmapped keys as `VC_UNDEFINED`, but looking at the modifier handling code, when only Fn changes it doesn't trigger any of the four mask branches, so no event gets emitted at all. That's a dead end. The right move is to make the Mac default Right Option and simply exclude Fn from the available keys on macOS rather than offering something that won't work. But I need to be transparent about this limitation instead of silently dropping it.

I'm updating the type definition to remove `'fn'` entirely from the ScribeKey union, which means adjusting the Mac key list to just right-option, right-ctrl, ctrl, and meta. The settings page will get a note explaining that macOS doesn't expose Fn to applications. And I need to handle the case where old settings might have stored 'fn' as a value, which the fallback logic should already cover since it won't be in the available list anymore.

Now I'm sketching out the state machine for scribe-keys.ts: tracking whether the chosen modifier is held down, when it was pressed, whether the arm callback has fired, if a take is currently latched from a tap, and whether another key was pressed while the modifier was held. The keydown handler needs to detect when the chosen modifier goes down, start an arming timer, and mark the state as spoiled if any other key is pressed—though latched takes shouldn't be cancelled by typing since the user might be dictating into another application. less than ARM_MS but nothing else was pressed, that counts as a deliberate tap of the bare modifier and should latch anyway. So on release, if it wasn't spoiled and we're still holding, we latch regardless of whether we've armed yet.

The logic becomes cleaner: if released before TAP_MS and not spoiled, latch; if released after TAP_MS while armed, finish; if spoiled at any point, cancel. This preserves the no-flash-on-Ctrl+C behavior since Ctrl+C spoils the modifier.

There's a trade-off though: accidentally pressing Right Option briefly could latch and open the mic, but that's the same behavior as Wispr, and the pill has an X to close it anyway.

Now I'm thinking through the different press modes — 'hold' releases always finish or cancel with no latch, 'toggle' acts on release when unspoiled regardless of duration, and 'latch' uses the combined rule I just outlined.

Defining the release handler... → arm, press again → finish. That's the global shortcut behavior: always a toggle, regardless of the `press` setting. For the arming timer, I'll use setTimeout to check if the key's still held and not spoiled after ARM_MS fires. The LONGEST_MS cap belongs in the renderer's store since it owns the audio, but I need the keys object to expose a `stopped()` method so the store can reset the latch when the user clicks the pill's check or X button.

The keys class needs to track when a take ends so the next key press starts fresh rather than trying to finish a dead one. I'm defining the public API with methods to apply settings, signal when a take stops, check if the hook is active, and close the connection. On macOS I'll call the accessibility trust check when arming and return that state so the UI can display it, since libuiohook requires accessibility permissions there.

The uiohook module is CommonJS, so I need to be careful about how I load it in the ESM main process—if the native module fails to load, the whole process crashes. I'll wrap the require in a try/catch and load it lazily instead of at import time. For tests, I need to drive the state machine by hand without the native module, so I'm extracting the pure logic into its own module that tests can use independently.

Writing the state machine module... Defining the state machine logic... Refining the state machine logic...

I'm spotting a bug in toggle mode where pressing when armed would emit 'finish' and set armed to false, but then release() would see armed as false and arm again. I need to track whether a press already completed its action with a consumed flag, so release() knows not to re-arm after the press has already finished.

In latch mode, pressing while latched should emit 'finish' and set consumed to true, so the release does nothing. For the stopped() method, I'm resetting armed and latched to false, and setting consumed based on whether the key is still held down to prevent re-finishing on release.

I'm also making hold mode only arm on tick, so a quick tap does nothing—which is the correct behavior for hold mode, even if it means someone holding for 150ms gets nothing.

+ import { ARM_MS, TAP_MS, type ScribePress } from './scribe'
+ 
+ // What one key does over time. It is numbers and nothing else, the way the games
+ // are: no keyboard, no timer of its own, no electron. Whatever is really
+ // listening feeds it presses and the clock, and it says what should happen.
+ //
+ // Four rules make a bare modifier bearable, and each one is here because without
+ // it the key is unusable. It does not arm until it has been held alone, so
+ // reaching for a shortcut never raises the pill. Any other key drops the take
+ // and lets the shortcut through. A tap latches, so a hold is a hold and a tap is
+ // hands free, which is one rule rather than a mode to pick. And a press while it
+ // is latched is what ends it.
+ 
+ export type LatchWord = 'nothing' | 'arm' | 'finish' | 'cancel'
+ 
+ export class ScribeLatch {
+   private down = false
+   private downAt = 0
+   private spoiled = false
+   private armed = false
+   private latched = false
+   // The press has already done its work, so the release that follows does none.
+   // Without it a toggle ends a take on the way down and opens another on the way
+   // back up, which reads as a key that cannot be turned off.
+   private spent = false
+ 
+   constructor(private press: ScribePress) {}
+ 
+   mode(press: ScribePress): void {
+     this.press = press
+   }
+ 
+   get running(): boolean {
+     return this.armed
+   }
+ 
+   get holding(): boolean {
+     return this.down
+   }
+ 
+   keyDown(at: number): LatchWord {
+     if (this.down) return 'nothing'
+     this.down = true
+     this.downAt = at
+     this.spoiled = false
+     this.spent = false
+     if (this.armed && (this.latched || this.press === 'toggle')) {
+       this.armed = false
+       this.latched = false
+       this.spent = true
+       return 'finish'
+     }
+     return 'nothing'
+   }
+ 
+   // The arming delay, come round. Nothing arms on the way down, so a key that
+   // turned out to be the front of a shortcut never opened a microphone.
+   tick(at: number): LatchWord {
+     if (!this.down || this.spoiled || this.spent || this.armed) return 'nothing'
+     if (this.press === 'toggle') return 'nothing'
+     if (at - this.downAt < ARM_MS) return 'nothing'
+     this.armed = true
+     this.latched = false
+     return 'arm'
+   }
+ 
+   // Anything else pressed while the key is held. This is the whole of what makes
+   // plain Control safe to dictate on.
+   other(): LatchWord {
+     if (!this.down || this.spoiled) return 'nothing'
+     this.spoiled = true
+     if (!this.armed) return 'nothing'
+     this.armed = false
+     this.latched = false
+     return 'cancel'
+   }
+

+ import { BrowserWindow, screen } from 'electron'
+ import type { ScribeSettings } from '../shared/scribe'
+ import type { PanelPage } from './tray-panel'
+ import { createScribeOptions } from './window-options'
+ 
+ // The pill, and the window it stands in. Frameless, transparent, above
+ // everything, and never focused: whatever you were typing in has to keep the
+ // caret, or a dictation would land nowhere.
+ 
+ const WIDTH = 216
+ const HEIGHT = 56
+ const MAX_HEIGHT = 140
+ // How far off the bottom of the screen it sits. Low enough to be out of the way
+ // and high enough to clear a dock.
+ const LIFT = 96
+ 
+ export class ScribeWindow {
+   private win: BrowserWindow | null = null
+   private settings: ScribeSettings | null = null
+ 
+   constructor(private readonly page: PanelPage) {}
+ 
+   owns(win: BrowserWindow): boolean {
+     return this.win === win
+   }
+ 
+   // Built and loaded before anyone presses the key, the way the tray panel is,
+   // and for a bigger reason: this window holds whisper, and a model that has to
+   // be fetched at the moment somebody starts talking is a first dictation that
+   // arrives a minute late.
+   warm(): void {
+     this.window()
+   }
+ 
+   show(): void {
+     const win = this.window()
+     this.place()
+     // Never `show`, which would take the focus off the app being dictated into
+     // and land the paste in the wrong place, or nowhere at all.
+     win.showInactive()
+   }
+ 
+   hide(): void {
+     this.win?.hide()
+   }
+ 
+   get showing(): boolean {
+     return this.win?.isVisible() ?? false
+   }
+ 
+   send(channel: string, ...args: unknown[]): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win || win.webContents.isDestroyed()) return
+     win.webContents.send(channel, ...args)
+   }
+ 
+   apply(settings: ScribeSettings): void {
+     this.settings = settings
+     this.send('scribe:settings', settings)
+   }
+ 
+   resize(height: number): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win) return
+     const wanted = Math.round(Math.max(HEIGHT, Math.min(height, MAX_HEIGHT)))
+     if (win.getBounds().height === wanted) return
+     win.setBounds({ ...win.getBounds(), height: wanted })
+     this.place()
+   }
+ 
+   close(): void {
+     this.win?.destroy()
+     this.win = null
+   }
+ 
+   // The screen the pointer is on rather than the primary one, because that is
+   // the screen the app being typed into is almost certainly on.
+   private place(): void {
+     const win = this.win
+     if (!win) return
+     const bounds = win.getBounds()
+     const work = screen.getDisplayNearestPoint(screen.getCursorScreenPoint()).workArea
+     win.setBounds({

Looking at some existing files to understand the code style, then examining how table-driven tests are structured. I'm thinking through the core algorithm: Whisper returns word-level chunks with timestamps, so I need to normalize these into tokens with trimmed text and position information.

My approach is to split each chunk by whitespace into individual words, then track gaps between chunks while treating gaps within chunks as zero. Each token will store the word itself, its start/end times, and the silence duration before it.

For handling fillers, I need to parse each token into its components—leading punctuation, the core word, and trailing punctuation—so that when I drop a filler word, I can cleanly remove it without leaving orphaned punctuation or double spaces.

When a filler is surrounded by commas (like "it was, like, huge"), dropping the filler should also remove one of the flanking commas to avoid leaving a stranded comma. For gap merging, when a filler token is dropped, I'll carry its gap forward to the next token using the maximum of the two gaps, since the silence around the filler is real even if the filler itself isn't.

Now I'm defining the core set of filler words to always drop: um, uh, uhh, er, erm, ah, mm, mmm, hmm, and huh, sticking closely to the specified list. For conditional asides like "you know," "I mean," "sort of," and similar phrases, I'll drop them only when they're clearly set off—either surrounded by commas or bracketed by pauses. I'm deciding to run the filler detection first on tokens with gaps, so I can recognize asides by pause timing as well as punctuation, using a threshold like 0.25 seconds to identify when something stands alone.

For "like" specifically, I'll drop it when there's a comma or pause both before and after it, or when it's followed by a comma—but I'll keep it in cases like "sort of blue" where there's no clear punctuation marking it as an aside. The test cases need to match the implementation exactly: "it was, like, huge" loses the "like," while "sort of blue" and "I mean it" stay intact.

For two-word phrases like "you know," I'll apply the same logic as a unit—drop when it's clearly set off as an aside with punctuation on both sides, but preserve it in phrases like "you know the answer" where it's integral to the meaning.

With "I mean," there's a potential ordering issue: correction phrases like "I mean no" need to be handled before the filler removal, otherwise dropping "I mean" first would break the correction. I should either run corrections before fillers or make fillers skip when "no" follows immediately. I'm working through the ordering of these processing steps. Running corrections before fillers seems cleaner since it avoids the problem where fillers might match parts of correction phrases. The tricky part is that corrections need to know where sentence boundaries are to cut back properly, and those boundaries are marked by gaps in the token stream. If I run fillers first, the token list gets cleaner but then corrections operate on raw tokens that still contain the filler words between phrase components, which could cause detection issues. I'm realizing fillers need to run before stutters because removing fillers can create new stutter patterns—like "the um the file" becoming "the the file" after filler removal. And corrections should come first to protect phrases like "I mean no" from being misidentified. So the order should be corrections, then fillers, then stutters, then marks, capitals, and dictionary.

There's a wrinkle with sentence boundary detection though: corrections cut back to the start of the current sentence using gaps, but if fillers create those gaps, running corrections first might split sentences awkwardly. Still, that's acceptable. The trickier case is something like "no wait for it"—if "no wait" triggers a correction cutback, it would delete everything back to the sentence start, leaving just "for the build to finish," which is what the task requires even if it feels risky.

To avoid false positives, I'll require the correction phrase to sit at a clear boundary: either at the sentence start, after punctuation, or after a noticeable pause. So "scratch that, let's use postgres" with commas works, but "say no wait for it" wouldn't trigger because "no" isn't preceded by a comma or pause—just the word "say." That keeps the logic sound.

The tricky part is handling natural speech where people might say "scratch that" quickly without a comma, or whisper might not always add punctuation. I'm thinking of loosening the boundary requirement to include gaps of 0.2 seconds or more, which would catch those natural pauses. But then there's the question of whether two-word phrases like "no wait" or "actually no" need stricter boundaries than longer phrases like "scratch that." Maybe I should keep it simple: let most phrases fire anywhere they appear as whole words, but apply the boundary rule only to the shorter, more ambiguous ones. I'll reuse that pause threshold across the board for consistency. For the correction logic, I need to handle both sentence-level deletions—which clear from the sentence start through the phrase—and whole-dictation deletions that wipe everything before and including the phrase. A sentence begins either after terminal punctuation or following a substantial pause.

When determining what counts as a sentence boundary, commas don't qualify, so "let's use redis, scratch that, let's use postgres" treats the whole thing as one sentence and removes only up through the phrase, leaving "let's use postgres." The phrase's trailing punctuation gets removed along with it.

Now I'm thinking through stutter detection—comparing repeated words case-insensitively while accounting for trailing marks, though cases like "I said no, no problem" complicate whether to flag them.
